## The Problem

Data on [Energy Certificates](https://epc.opendatacommunities.org/) were downloaded in March 2025. These certificates are a non-random sample of UK housing, and contain information such as:

- Property energy efficiency: The core data is the energy efficiency rating, which ranges from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient).
- CO2 emissions: The data includes information on the building's likely carbon dioxide emissions.
- Energy costs: Potential costs for heating and lighting the property are provided.
- Improvement recommendations: Each EPC lists cost-effective ways to improve the building's energy performance.

In all, 93 variables are available across a wide range of energy and property metrics. For this analysis, a subset of seven energy-related variables was extracted from the course database.

The data have been used for various published supervised classification exercises:

- ONS data science campus EPC data to predict energy efficiency ratings across Welsh properties. They applied models like XGBoost and found that features such as floor area, number of habitable rooms, and extension count were most predictive <https://datasciencecampus.ons.gov.uk/projects/using-machine-learning-to-predict-energy-efficiency/>
- EPC anomaly detection (improve data quality) <https://www.iaarc.org/publications/fulltext/102_A_Comprehensive_Approach_for_Automated_Anomaly_Detection_and_Enhancement_of_EPC_Datasets_for_Decarbonization.pdf>
- Identifying priorities for retrofit strategy <https://uwlpress.uwl.ac.uk/newvistas/article/id/299/>
- EPC prediction <https://github.com/yourunclefrankie/Energy-efficiency-prediction>

In reducing the carbon footprint of UK housing, it is important to develop a strategy that offers the right solutions to the right properties. It is widely believed that houses built before 1930 require very different approaches to houses built after that period.  In this task, you are required to determine whether it is possible to determine the age of a house based on several recorded energy metrics. These are `current_energy_efficiency`, `environment_impact_current`, `energy_consumption_current`, `co2_emissions_current`, `lighting_cost_current`, `heating_cost_current`, `hot_water_cost_current`.  You have data for all certificates issued in a single local authority area.  This would help the local authority identify the right targets just using metrics rather than requiring a visit to the property to determine its age.


The dataset contains 66,987 properties: 36,523 classified as pre-1930 and 30,464 as post-1930. Pre-1930 properties generally have poorer energy performance. Their mean current energy-efficiency rating is 51.7, compared with 63.6 for post-1930 properties, while their mean environmental-impact rating is also lower at 47.3 compared with 60.5.

Older properties also have higher average energy consumption, carbon emissions and heating costs. Mean heating cost is approximately £1,303 for pre-1930 properties, compared with £831 for post-1930 properties. However, lighting and hot-water costs are relatively similar between the groups. These differences suggest that the selected energy variables contain useful information for predicting whether a property was built before 1930.


The scatterplot below shows the relationships between the energy variables, with the two known age groups marked separately.

![](../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/scatterplot.html){width="100%" height="600px"}



The scatterplot shows considerable overlap between the two age groups, meaning that no individual energy variable provides a perfect separation. However, the combined differences across efficiency, environmental impact, consumption, emissions and heating costs suggest that classification using several variables may still be effective.


## Fitting LDA and QDA classifiers

The simplest classifiers we could apply are Linear and Quadratic Discriminant analysis.


```{python}
#| echo: false
#| results: 'asis'
df = pd.read_csv('../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/lda.csv')
df.rename(columns={"Unnamed: 0": "Category"}, inplace=True)
print(df.round(3).to_markdown(index=False))
```

### Results from fitting a quadratic discriminant analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| results: 'asis'
df = pd.read_csv('../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/qda.csv')
df.rename(columns={"Unnamed: 0": "Category"}, inplace=True)
print(df.round(3).to_markdown(index=False))
```

LDA performs better overall than QDA. LDA achieves an accuracy of 0.738 and a weighted F1-score of 0.737. Its performance is reasonably balanced across the two classes, with recall values of 0.682 for post-1930 properties and 0.784 for pre-1930 properties.

QDA achieves a lower accuracy of 0.626 and a weighted F1-score of 0.608. Its predictions are also less balanced. Although it identifies 88.5% of post-1930 properties, it identifies only 41.2% of pre-1930 properties. Therefore, QDA frequently classifies older properties as post-1930.

These results indicate that the simpler linear decision boundary used by LDA is more suitable for this dataset than the more flexible quadratic boundary used by QDA.


## ROC curve (and AUC) for two simple classifiers

We can of course examine the AUC for these classifiers.


![](../../data_cache/vignettes/supervised_classification/roc.html){width="100%" height="600px"}


Both ROC curves lie clearly above the diagonal random-classification line, showing that both models have useful discriminatory ability. LDA has an AUC of 0.81, compared with 0.79 for QDA. This supports the earlier performance metrics and indicates that LDA is slightly better at distinguishing between pre-1930 and post-1930 properties across different classification thresholds.

Overall, the selected energy metrics provide a useful indication of whether a property was built before 1930. However, the LDA accuracy of approximately 74% means that around one quarter of properties are still misclassified. The model could therefore support initial targeting by a local authority, but it should not replace definitive property records or an inspection when an accurate age classification is required.
